{{Short description|Vengeful Japanese ghosts}}
{{about|the mythological Japanese spirit|the Korean dynasty|Goryeo}}{{Expand Japanese}}[[File:Tsukioka (Taiso) Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Sugawara no Michizane roept een onweersbui op boven KyotoKôkoku (1880).jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|[[Ukiyo-e]]}} by {{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|qid=Q467337|lt=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} depicting {{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|en|Sugawara no Michizane|qid=Q382005|lt=Sugawara no Michizane}} as the {{nihongo3|{{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of thunder.||{{ill|Tenjin (kami)|en|Tenjin (kami)|qid=Q1753428|lt=Tenjin}}}}. After Sugawara no Michizane's death, lightning struck the palace, killing and injuring many of the powerful people involved in his banishment, and Sugawara no Michizane was enshrined in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Tenmangū]]}} ({{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}}) as the Tenjin.]]
In a broad sense, {{nihongo|'''Goryō'''|[[Wiktionary:御霊|御霊]]||{{IPA|ja|ɡoɾʲoː|lang}}}}  is an honorific for a spirit, especially one that causes hauntings, and the term is used as a synonym for {{nihongo3|{{ill|Vengeful ghost|en|Vengeful ghost|qid=Q2836709|lt=vengeful}} {{ill|Yūrei|en|Yūrei|qid=Q11050647|lt=Japanese ghosts}}|怨霊|[[onryō]]}}. In a narrower sense, it refers to a person who was a noble or accomplished person in his or her lifetime, but who lost a political power struggle or died prematurely from an epidemic or other disease, becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} that brings pestilence or famine and is later enshrined as a {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} in {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}}. For example, the "[[:en:Sandai Jitsuroku|Sandai Jitsuroku]]" (a historical Japanese document) mentions that six Shinto shrines were dedicated to the worship of {{transliteration|ja|goryō}}, which were the spirits of those who died from non-natural causes. Later on, two more shrines were added, bringing the total to eight.<ref name="kotogoryo">{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025142/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|script-title=ja:御霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kotoshinko">{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|script-title=ja:御霊信仰|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|script-title=ja:怨霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>

{{nihongo3|Belief in ''goryō''|[[:ja:御霊信仰|御霊信仰]]|Goryō Shinko}} refers to the belief that the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} of people who have died unfortunate deaths cause hauntings and disasters, and the belief that they are enshrined as {{transliteration|ja|kami}} to appease them.<ref name="kotoshinko"/>

==Description==
The name consists of two {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|qid=Q82772|lt=Kanji}}, 御 (go) meaning honorable and 霊 (ryō) meaning soul or spirit.

In Japan, the belief that the soul leaves the body as a spirit upon death has existed since ancient times, as evidenced by practices such as flexed burial (屈葬) during the {{ill|Jōmon period|en|Jōmon period|qid=Q52824|lt=Jōmon period}}. From this foundational belief arose the idea that these spirits could bring various calamities to the living.

The belief that the spirits of those who died with resentment or anger after being treated unfairly caused hauntings existed before the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} (710–794). However, from the Nara to the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}s (794–1185), the belief arose that the spirits of those who died after being defeated in a power struggle among the nobility caused plagues and natural disasters, and {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} were built to appease their spirits and enshrine them as {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}}. The first example is {{ill|Prince Sawara|en|Prince Sawara|qid=Q1079634|lt=Prince Sawara}}, who was stripped of his position as crown prince and exiled to {{ill|Awaji Island|en|Awaji Island|qid=Q504373|lt=Awaji Island}} to die in 785. After his death, a plague epidemic broke out in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, which people feared was caused by his spirit. So the Kamigoryo Shrine ([[:ja:上御霊神社|ja]]) was built in Kyoto in 794 to appease his spirit, and he was enshrined as a {{transliteration|ja|kami}}.<ref name="kotoshinko"/>

The idea that arose through the Heian period was that if one restored a vengeful spirit to its former position, bestowed posthumous titles and court ranks, calmed its spirit, and enshrined it as a kami, the spirit would be pacified as a ''goryō'' and provide protection and peace rather than bringing harm. Also, the {{nihongo|''goryo-e''|御霊会}} (ceremony for the ''goryō'') was performed as a court ritual for this purpose. The first ''goryo-e'' recorded in historical sources was held at Shinsen'en on the 20th day of the 5th month in 863 (Jōgan 5), as documented in the ''[[:en:Sandai Jitsuroku|Sandai Jitsuroku]]''.

At this first ''goryo-e'', six individuals were enshrined: Emperor Sudō (崇道天皇, Prince Sawara), Prince Iyo (伊予親王), the Fujiwara Lady (藤原大夫人, Fujiwara no Yoshiko), Tachibana no Hayanari (橘逸勢), Funya no Miyatamaro (文室宮田麻呂), and the ''kansatsu-shi'' (either Fujiwara no Nakanari or Fujiwara no Hirotsugu). Later, Empress Inoue, Prince Osabe, Kaminari Tenjin, and Kibi Seiryō were added while two of the original six were removed, forming the "Eight Goryō" (八所御霊) enshrined at the Goryō Shrines ({{ill|Kamigoryo Shrine|ja|上御霊神社|qid=Q11359018|lt=Kamigoryo Shrine}} and {{ill|Shimogoryo Shrine|ja|下御霊神社|qid=Q11360904|lt=Shimogoryo Shrine}}).

An example of a {{transliteration|ja|goryō}} is the [[kami|Shinto kami]] known as {{ill|Tenjin (kami)|en|Tenjin (kami)|qid=Q1753428|lt=Tenjin}}:
<blockquote>
Government official {{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|en|Sugawara no Michizane|qid=Q382005|lt=Sugawara no Michizane}} was killed in a plot by a rival member of the [[Fujiwara clan]]. In the years after his death, the capital city was struck by heavy rain and lightning, and his chief Fujiwara adversary and {{ill|Emperor Daigo|en|Emperor Daigo|qid=Q329753|lt=Emperor Daigo}}'s crown prince died, while fires caused by lightning and floods destroyed many residences. The court drew the conclusion that the disturbances were caused by Michizane's {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}. In order to placate him, the emperor restored all his offices, burned the official order of exile, and he was promoted to Senior Second Rank. Even this wasn't enough, and 70 years later he was elevated to the post of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|qid=Q1157586|lt=Daijō-daijin}}, and he was deified as Tenjin-sama, which means "heavenly deity". He became the patron god of calligraphy, of poetry and of those who suffer injustice. A shrine was established at Kitano. With the support of the government, it was immediately raised to the first Rank of official shrines.<ref>Morris, 54.</ref></blockquote>

From the Heian to the Kamakura period, {{ill|Emperor Sutoku|en|Emperor Sutoku|qid=Q349287|lt=Emperor Sutoku}}, Fujiwara no Yorinaga (the Evil Left Minister of Uji), Emperor Antoku, Retired Emperor Go-Toba, Retired Emperor Juntoku, and Emperor Go-Daigo were feared as having become vengeful spirits, and the court and shogunate built temples and shrines to appease and memorialize them. Through the Northern and Southern Courts period, such appeasement of vengeful spirits increasingly incorporated Buddhist elements, but ''goryō shinko'' had not declined. The ''Taiheiki'', while under Buddhist influence, presents the turmoil of the Northern and Southern Courts as the work of vengeful spirits and regards them as the driving force of social change—a further development of the way in which the ''Hōgen Monogatari'' and ''Heike Monogatari'' attribute part of the cause of the Genpei War's upheaval to the vengeful spirit of Retired Emperor Sutoku.

==Gion Faith==
[[Image:Yasaka Jinja.jpg|thumb|250px|right|{{ill|Yasaka Shrine|ja|八坂神社|qid=Q692714|lt=Yasaka Shrine}}]]
Related to ''goryō shinko'' is the belief in pestilence deities (疫神信仰, ''ekijin shinko''). This is the practice of venerating plague deities—the smallpox deity and the cold deity—to ward off disease, and is similar to ''goryō shinko'' in character. The most famous and nationwide example is Gion faith, which venerates {{ill|Gozu Tennō|ja|牛頭天王|qid=Q11570247|lt=Gozu Tennō}} (the Ox-Head Heavenly King). Gozu Tennō, as a bringer of disease and misfortune, is enshrined at {{ill|Yasaka Shrine|ja|八坂神社|qid=Q692714|lt=Yasaka Shrine}} in Kyoto, giving rise to Gion faith. Many shrines throughout Japan called Yasaka Shrine, Gion Shrine, or Yakumo Shrine once enshrined Gozu Tennō. However, due to the religious policies of the Meiji era, {{ill|Susanoo|en|Susanoo|qid=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} is now enshrined as the main deity at many of these in place of Gozu Tennō.

The present {{ill|Gion Festival|ja|祇園祭|qid=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} also arose from this faith in Gozu Tennō.

==Other==
Because the sound of ''goryō'' resembles that of "Gorō (五郎)," many things bearing the name "Gorō" are found, such as the {{ill|Goryō Shrine (Kamakura)|ja|御霊神社 (鎌倉市)|qid=Q11489364|lt=Kamakura Gongorō Shrine}} and the {{nihongo|Yagoro-don Festival|弥五郎どん祭り}} seen from Kagoshima Prefecture's Ōsumi Peninsula to southern Miyazaki Prefecture.

Throughout Japan, mounds called "Gorōzuka" and similar names are said to be corruptions of "Goryō-zuka" (vengeful spirit mounds). This too is a form of ''goryō shinko''.

{{ill|Yanagita Kunio|en|Yanagita Kunio|qid=Q971687|lt=Yanagita Kunio}} put forward the theory regarding the graves of the Soga Brothers, scattered throughout various regions, that "the graves of vengeful spirits may have become the graves of Soga Gorō through the spread of the Soga Brothers story."
